In [[theoretical computer science]], and specifically [[computational complexity theory]] and [[circuit complexity]], '''TC''' (Threshold Circuit) is a [[complexity class]] of [[Decision problem|decision problems]] that can be recognized by threshold circuits, which are [[Boolean circuit]]s with [[AND gate|AND]], [[OR gate|OR]], and [[Majority gate]]s, or equivalently, [[Threshold Logic Unit|threshold gates]]. For each fixed ''i'', the complexity class '''TC<sup>i</sup>''' consists of all languages that can be recognized by a family of threshold circuits of depth <math>O(\log^i n)</math>, [[polynomial]] size, and unbounded [[fan-in]]. The class '''TC''' is defined via
:<math>\mbox{TC} = \bigcup_{i \geq 0} \mbox{TC}^i.</math>
The class was proposed in 1988 to formalize the computational complexity of [[Neural network (machine learning)|artificial neural networks]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parberry |first1=Ian |last2=Schnitger |first2=Georg |date=June 1988 |title=Parallel computation with threshold functions |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/002200008890030X |journal=Journal of Computer and System Sciences |language=en |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=278–302 |doi=10.1016/0022-0000(88)90030-X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Relation to NC and AC==
The relationship between the TC, [[NC (complexity)|NC]] and the [[AC (complexity)|AC]] hierarchy can be summarized as follows:
:<math>\mbox{NC}^i \subseteq \mbox{AC}^i \subseteq \mbox{TC}^i \subseteq \mbox{NC}^{i+1}.</math>

In particular, we know that
:<math>\mbox{NC}^0 \subsetneq \mbox{AC}^0 \subsetneq \mbox{TC}^0 \subseteq \mbox{NC}^{1}.</math>

The first strict containment follows from the fact that '''NC<sup>0</sup>''' cannot compute any function that depends on all the input bits. Thus choosing a problem that is trivially in '''AC<sup>0</sup>''' and depends on all bits separates the two classes. (For example, consider the OR function.) The strict containment '''AC<sup>0</sup>''' ⊊ '''TC<sup>0</sup>''' follows because parity and majority (which are both in '''TC<sup>0</sup>''') were shown to be not in '''AC<sup>0</sup>'''.<ref>{{citation | last1 = Furst | first1 = Merrick | last2 = Saxe | first2 = James B. | author2-link = James B. Saxe | last3 = Sipser | first3 = Michael | author3-link = Michael Sipser | doi = 10.1007/BF01744431 | issue = 1 | journal = Mathematical Systems Theory | mr = 738749 | pages = 13–27 | title = Parity, circuits, and the polynomial-time hierarchy | volume = 17 | year = 1984}}.</ref><ref>{{Citation | last1=Håstad | first1=Johan | series=Advances in Computing Research | volume=5 | title=Randomness and Computation | editor-first=Silvio | editor-last=Micali | url=http://reference.kfupm.edu.sa/content/a/l/almost_optimal_lower_bounds_for_small_de_134215.pdf | publisher=JAI Press | year=1989 | chapter=Almost Optimal Lower Bounds for Small Depth Circuits | pages=6–20 | isbn=0-89232-896-7 | url-status=dead | archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120222163102/http://reference.kfupm.edu.sa/content/a/l/almost_optimal_lower_bounds_for_small_de_134215.pdf | archivedate=2012-02-22 }}</ref>

As an immediate consequence of the above containments, we have that NC = AC = TC.
